name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,735

clue.text: "Simply thunderous shot! Unbelievable Jeff - leaders turned over!"

indicators.note: leaders are the ones at the front, so only each word's opening letter is kept
something turned over ends up the other way round, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: first letter
first letter
first letter
first letter

explanation.surface: Jeff Stelling, the Sky Sports presenter, gasping at a thunderbolt goal as he did on Soccer Saturday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unbelievable, Jeff!' was the catchphrase of pundit Chris Kamara on Sky's Soccer Saturday, which this whole puzzle celebrates. The first letters read TSUJ, then flip.
explanation.definitionFit: Both work as adverbs meaning merely or only, as in 'it was simply a joke'.

clue.text: Aim to publish supportive column

blocks.note: an aim is a target or objective
to post a notice is to publish it

explanation.surface: A newspaper editor deciding to run an opinion piece backing someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supportive column' reads like a friendly newspaper article; it is really an upright holding up a crossbar.
explanation.definitionFit: Each upright of a football goal is a vertical post that holds the crossbar up, a literal supporting pillar.

clue.text: Alpha male Stelling’s outside receiving thanks

indicators.note: the outside of a word is its two ends, so only the outer letters are kept
to receive is to take something in, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the presenter's surname
ta is informal British for thanks

explanation.surface: Jeff Stelling, the dominant figure of the studio, being thanked by his panel.
explanation.walkthrough: Ta is everyday British slang for thank you.
explanation.definitionFit: A mature male deer that leads the herd is the classic image of dominance, the original alpha male.

clue.text: For Spooner, really tedious American's an easy target

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts of two words trade places

blocks.note: darn is a mild intensifier meaning really, common in American speech; it takes the other word's opening sound
a bore is a tedious person; it takes the first word's opening sound

explanation.surface: Someone dull from the States makes an easy mark for mockery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Darn' is the polite American swear meaning very; with 'bore' it gives a darn bore, whose initial sounds swapped make the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase 'couldn't hit a barn door' describes poor aim, because the side of a barn is a huge target nobody should miss.

clue.text: A sport broadcast hit - entertaining revelry, principally

indicators.note: principally means first and foremost, so only the opening letters count
what is broadcast is heard rather than seen, so the sound matters, not the spelling

blocks.note: to sock someone is to punch them; said with what follows, it is heard as the first syllable
the first letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A televised sporting smash hit full of fun and partying.
explanation.walkthrough: Sock plus ER makes 'socker', which is pronounced exactly like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Association football is widely called by this name, particularly in North America, where football means a different game.

clue.text: Compassionate giant's visitor admitted violent theft

indicators.note: to be admitted is to be let inside, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: compassionate means kind and caring
in the fairy tale Jack climbs the beanstalk to visit the giant

explanation.surface: A kindly giant lets in a guest who turns out to be a violent robber.
explanation.walkthrough: The giant's visitor is Jack of 'Jack and the Beanstalk', who climbed up and stole from him.
explanation.definitionFit: Seizing a motor vehicle from its driver by force or threats is a crime of robbery with violence.

clue.text: Music on alien spacecraft

blocks.note: rock is a style of music
ET is the film alien, the Extra-Terrestrial

explanation.surface: Tunes playing aboard a flying saucer.
explanation.walkthrough: ET, from the Spielberg film, is the standard crossword alien.
explanation.definitionFit: A vehicle propelled by burning fuel to escape the atmosphere is the usual kind of craft sent into orbit.

clue.text: Dismiss account from person blaming addict

indicators.note: to dismiss is to send away, so these letters are thrown out of the longer word

blocks.note: acc. is the abbreviation for account
someone who blames another accuses them

explanation.surface: Rejecting the story of someone pointing the finger at a drug addict.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Account' looks like a story to be dismissed; it is the abbreviation ACC, struck from the front of ACCUSER.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who habitually takes drugs is commonly called by this shorter informal term.

clue.text: Wartime fighter in regular display of dumb loyalty

indicators.note: regular means at even intervals, so every other letter is shown

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters

explanation.surface: A soldier at war shows unquestioning devotion to the cause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fighter' suggests a soldier or a plane; it is a submarine.
explanation.definitionFit: German submarines attacked Allied shipping in both world wars, so they were combatants in naval warfare.

clue.text: Freak loves to become absorbed in fighting manuals

indicators.note: whatever is absorbed is taken right inside, so one set of letters goes in among the others
fighting things are thrown about and jumbled, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: love is zero in tennis, written O; two of them
taken as written

explanation.surface: An oddball loses himself in reading combat handbooks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Freak' looks like a noun but is an adjective here, as in freak weather; love is O from tennis scoring.
explanation.definitionFit: A freak event is abnormal or unusual, deviating from what is expected.

clue.text: Good to watch: Terry Butcher in Greece skipping about

indicators.note: to skip something is to leave it out, so those letters are dropped
a butcher chops things up, so the letters are hacked into a new order

blocks.note: Tel is the familiar short form of Terry
taken as written
taken as written
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: Terry Butcher, the England defender turned pundit, is worth watching in a match in Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: Terry Butcher looks like one name; 'Butcher' is the anagram signal. GREECE without RE leaves GECE, mixed with TEL and IN.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who comes across well on television screens is appealing to viewers, pleasant to look at.

clue.text: Royal couple touched by Jack Nicholson’s core wit

indicators.note: the core is the very centre, so only the middle letter is taken

blocks.note: J is the jack in a pack of cards
the fifth of nine letters
K for king and ER for the queen, Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: Jack Nicholson's comic genius moves the royals, and he of course played the Joker in Batman.
explanation.walkthrough: The royal couple is K (king) and ER (Elizabeth Regina), and they sit after the other letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A wit is a person who makes clever jokes, so a funny prankster fits the noun.

clue.text: Cut short noisy party beside a tree

indicators.note: cutting something short trims off its end, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: taken as written
vocal means loud and outspoken
a do is a party

explanation.surface: Someone ends a rowdy party early, next to a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut short' wants to mean ending the party early; it applies only to the word for noisy. A do is a party.
explanation.definitionFit: The pear-shaped fruit grows on an evergreen tropical plant of the laurel family, known by the same name.

clue.text: Sir Alex Ferguson? He's one for the races!

blocks.note: one means a single, so A
the Manchester United manager is from Glasgow

explanation.surface: Sir Alex Ferguson, a famous racehorse owner, is a man who loves a day at the races.
explanation.walkthrough: Ascot is a famous English racecourse, home of Royal Ascot. 'He's one' turns the Scot into a Scot.
explanation.definitionFit: The Berkshire racecourse hosts Royal Ascot, so going there means attending horse racing meetings.

clue.text: Sky veteran, alarm disguised, keeps quiet after broadcast

indicators.note: a disguise changes how something looks, so the letters appear in a new order
to keep something is to hold it inside, so one piece goes within the other
after places one piece behind another in the reading order

blocks.note: to air a programme is to broadcast it
taken as written
sh is the call for quiet

explanation.surface: A long-serving Sky Sports man hides his panic and stays calm on air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sky' suggests the broadcaster, as throughout this puzzle; here it is the literal sky, home of an air force.
explanation.definitionFit: A senior Royal Air Force officer is an experienced commander of operations in the sky, hence a veteran of the air.

clue.text: Reels off transfers for audience

indicators.note: an audience listens, so what matters is how the word is heard

blocks.note: to re-site something is to move it to a new place

explanation.surface: A transfer list being read out to watching fans.
explanation.walkthrough: Transfers here are not football signings but relocations: re-sites.
explanation.definitionFit: To reel off a list is to say it from memory, quickly and fluently, as one does a poem.

clue.text: Offensive Aunt open to criticism?

blocks.note: first meaning: a sudden attack out of a besieged place, a sortie
second meaning: completes the phrase for a target of everyone's abuse

explanation.walkthrough: 'Offensive' reads as an adjective describing the aunt; it is a noun, an attack. An Aunt Sally is a British fairground figure people throw things at, hence any easy target of criticism.
explanation.definitionFit: A military sortie is a sudden charge, and an Aunt Sally is the stock figure people pelt with blame.

clue.text: Water tube cutting out the supply

indicators.note: to cut something out is to remove it, so those letters are taken away

blocks.note: a thin tube that drains urine from the bladder
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pipe being cut off, stopping the water supply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Water' is a medical euphemism here, making the tube a catheter rather than a plumbing pipe.
explanation.definitionFit: To provide food and drink for an event, or to meet people's needs, is to furnish or provide them.

clue.text: Fine follows - concerning for whistle-blower

indicators.note: what follows comes behind, setting the order of the two pieces

blocks.note: re means concerning
F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A penalty is imposed on someone who leaked secrets.
explanation.walkthrough: A whistle-blower usually exposes wrongdoing; here it is the official with the whistle.
explanation.definitionFit: The football referee blows a whistle to stop play, so he is literally one who blows it.

clue.text: Animated old Jeff, outwardly lacking ego, bringing joy

indicators.note: lacking the outside means the two end letters are missing
animated means set in lively motion, so the letters move about

blocks.note: taken as written
the name without its first and last letters
taken as written

explanation.surface: Jeff Stelling, older now, lively and modest, still cheering everyone up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lacking ego' looks like one phrase; split it, as 'outwardly lacking' works on Jeff and EGO is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Something cheerful and uplifting that leaves people happy is described with this adjective, as in a feel-good film.

clue.text: Cheeky devil lying about the French press

indicators.note: something lying about has been turned round, so the letters face the other way

blocks.note: an imp is a mischievous little devil
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A brazen rogue fibbing to the newspapers in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press' looks like a noun meaning newspapers; it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To press someone into acting is to urge or drive them forward, the same as compelling them.

clue.text: Pundits supported by gallery's fluid production system

indicators.note: in a down entry what is supported sits on top, so this piece comes first

blocks.note: pundits are experts, or pros
the Tate is the London art gallery

explanation.surface: TV pundits backed up by an art gallery's well-run production line.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tate is the famous London art gallery; the cryptic definition hints at a gland, not a factory.
explanation.definitionFit: This male gland secretes the fluid that carries sperm, a jokey way of calling it a liquid-making organ.

clue.text: Opera left English with an accurate perspective

blocks.note: Tosca is Puccini's opera
L is the abbreviation for left
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: An English opera-goer leaves with a clear and balanced view of the show.
explanation.walkthrough: Tosca by Puccini is the opera most often used in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: A drawing done in true proportion shows every part at the correct relative size.

clue.text: Excited goons taking in football - finally it's farewell

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so just the last letter is kept
excited things are stirred up, so the letters are mixed
to take in is to hold inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: taken as written
the final letter

explanation.surface: Overexcited hooligans at a match get kicked out for good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goons' looks like the subject of the sentence, but the word is only letters to be stirred, with the end of football dropped into them.
explanation.definitionFit: This casual interjection is a way of saying goodbye when parting from someone.

clue.text: Secretly monitor creepy-crawly

blocks.note: first meaning: a British verb, to eavesdrop on a conversation
second meaning: an insect with pincers at its tail

explanation.walkthrough: As a verb this is informal British for listening in on others; the surface suggests a bug planted to spy.
explanation.definitionFit: The pincered insect is a typical small crawling creature, and the verb means to eavesdrop furtively.

clue.text: Cover provided until the soldiers arrive?

definitions.text: Cover provided until the soldiers arrive?

blocks.clueFragment: Cover provided until the soldiers arrive?
blocks.note: surface reading: troops holding a position until reinforcements turn up
setter's reading: soldiers are strips of toast dipped in a boiled egg, which is kept warm under a knitted cover until they are ready

explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'soldiers' are fingers of buttered toast served with a soft-boiled egg.
explanation.definitionFit: A padded cap placed over a boiled egg keeps it hot while breakfast toast is prepared.

clue.text: Degree students essentially rehashing nonsense

indicators.note: the essence of a thing is at its heart, so the central letter is taken

blocks.note: BA is a Bachelor of Arts degree
L is a learner, so two learners
the fifth of nine letters

explanation.surface: A university course where students just recycle rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: L for learner (from L-plates) gives the students.
explanation.definitionFit: This is vulgar British slang for rubbish talk, as in 'what a load of'.

clue.text: Delight in sport having rejected ballet dancing

indicators.note: dancing moves things around, so the letters change places
what is rejected is cast out, so those letters are removed

blocks.note: a sport played with hoops
the letters reordered

explanation.surface: A sporty person who turned down ballet lessons enjoys their game.
explanation.walkthrough: Shuffled 'ballet' gives the tail of BASKETBALL, which is then dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: To revel in praise or attention is to take great pleasure from it, like lying in the sun.

clue.text: Controlled German repulsed by wild adult popping ecstasy

indicators.note: repulsed means driven back, so the letters go backwards
popping in means slipping inside, so one letter enters the other word
wild means out of control, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: Ger. is the abbreviation for German
taken as written
E is the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A disciplined German is repelled by a raving grown-up taking drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: E is the standard abbreviation for the drug ecstasy; it goes into ADULT before the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Something governed by rules or kept in check is regulated, the same past-participle sense.

clue.text: Son, consumed by circumstances, vanished

indicators.note: what is consumed is swallowed up, so it ends up inside the other piece

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for son
one's lot is one's situation in life

explanation.surface: A boy overwhelmed by events disappears.
explanation.walkthrough: Lot means one's fortune or situation, as in 'happy with his lot'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that has disappeared and cannot be found is missing, gone from sight.

clue.text: European recalled Grenadier Guards

indicators.note: recalled means called back, so the letters run back the other way

blocks.note: letters inside the first word

explanation.surface: A foreign soldier is summoned back to a British army regiment.
explanation.walkthrough: The Grenadier Guards are a British Army regiment; read 'grENADier' backwards. There is no separate hiding signal, so the reversal word does both jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Denmark is a citizen of that Scandinavian country on the continent.

clue.text: Churchgoing sad anachronism in small country

indicators.note: something going is leaving, so those letters disappear from the longer word
sad can mean sorry or in a poor state, so the letters are a mess

blocks.note: church is shortened to CH as usual; the word glued on its end is the signal to remove it
taken as written

explanation.surface: Going to church is a sorry relic of the past in some little nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Churchgoing' reads as one word; split it into CH and the signal that it goes.
explanation.definitionFit: This tiny enclaved republic inside Italy is one of the smallest sovereign states in Europe.

clue.text: Silky sequence of passes at Internazionale

indicators.note: a sequence is a run of consecutive items, so the letters are read straight through the words

blocks.note: running across the word breaks

explanation.surface: Inter Milan stringing together a smooth, slick passing move.
explanation.walkthrough: Internazionale is Inter Milan, the Italian football club; the letters span the end of 'passes', 'at' and the start of the club.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective this describes a smooth glossy finish, like the fabric itself.
